answer.label: Not Albert Einstein — actually William Bruce Cameron
answer.sourceLine: The combined maxim appears in sociologist William Bruce Cameron’s 1963 textbook Informal Sociology: A Casual Introduction to Sociological Thinking (Random House). Cameron had used the first half by 1957; Quote Investigator finds no link to Einstein until 1986, three decades after his death.

source.heading: Where it actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Informal Sociology: A Casual Introduction to Sociological Thinking
First recorded 1986 — 31 years after Einstein died

source.excerpt: “It would be nice if all of the data which sociologists require could be enumerated because then we could run them through IBM machines and draw charts as the economists do. However, not everything that can be counted counts, and not everything that counts can be counted.”
trail: By 1957 Cameron had published the first half alone — “not everything that can be counted counts” — in the AAUP Bulletin, per Quote Investigator.
The full two-part maxim is printed in his 1963 book Informal Sociology, the wording preserved on Goodreads and tagged “misattributed-to-einstein.”
History.com lists it among things “Einstein never said,” noting he “wasn’t associated with the saying until the mid-1980s.”
source.excerptNote: Cameron’s 1963 wording runs “counted counts … counts can be counted”; the popular Einstein version simply swaps the order of the two halves.
source.rightsHolder: Estate of William Bruce Cameron / Random House
source.rightsNote: The line was first published in Cameron’s Informal Sociology (Random House, 1963), so under U.S. law it remains in copyright. The underlying idea is Cameron’s; the Einstein attribution is unsupported.

author.name: William Bruce Cameron
author.heading: About William Bruce Cameron
author.metaLine: American sociologist · author of Informal Sociology (1963)
author.bio: William Bruce Cameron was an American sociologist and educator. He used the phrase “not everything that can be counted counts” in professional journals in the late 1950s and folded it into the full chiastic maxim in his 1963 textbook Informal Sociology: A Casual Introduction to Sociological Thinking. The line, warning against mistaking the measurable for the meaningful, became his best-known legacy — ironically, mostly under someone else’s name.

misattribution.heading: Why everyone says Einstein
misattribution.intro: A quotable line about the limits of measurement, pinned to physics’ most famous name — a textbook case of a “quote magnet.”

items.why: No Einstein letter, essay, or lecture contains this line. Per Quote Investigator, the earliest Einstein connection is a 1986 book (Peak Performers) claiming he chalked it on his blackboard — 31 years after he died.

items.who: The reordered “counts can be counted…” version
items.why: Cameron’s 1963 text reads “not everything that can be counted counts, and not everything that counts can be counted.” The popular Einstein version swaps the two halves, but the substance is identical.

misattribution.truthLine: Credit the sociologist, not the physicist: William Bruce Cameron, Informal Sociology (1963), as documented by Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why the line stuck
lead: The maxim uses antimetabole — reversing “counted” and “counts” across two clauses — which makes it feel both clever and profound. That memorability, plus its message that the truly important often resists measurement, is exactly why it drifted from a working sociologist onto Einstein’s name.

Quote Investigator notes several intermediate figures who were credited over the years — Stephen Ross, Hilliard Jason, Lord Platt, George Pickering — before the Einstein version took over in the late 1980s and swamped them all.
